title: # Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach
content:
Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach

This survey presents the multifaceted figure of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, who is considered a pillar of the halakhic world in the twentieth century due to his unique ability to bridge the yeshiva tradition and the challenges of modernity. The text traces the trajectory of his life from his roots in Jerusalem to his transformation into a supreme halakhic authority, focusing on his innovative approach to questions of technology, medicine, and ethics based on deep scientific research. Beyond his halakhic leadership, the source emphasizes his educational work characterized by love of humanity and simplicity, and describes how his humble personality made him a living bridge between the different streams in religious and Haredi Judaism. The purpose of the composition is to illuminate the legacy of the "posek ha-dor" as one who proved that Torah and halakha are capable of renewing themselves and responding to changing reality without losing their deep roots.

Posek Ha-Dor in the Modern Era: The Halakhic Teachings, Educational Work, and Public Leadership of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach

In the Torah world of the twentieth century, the figure of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach (1910–1995) stands as a central pillar bridging the ancient yeshiva tradition and the challenges of modernity, technology, and advanced medicine. Rabbi Auerbach, called by all "HaGRaSh"Z" or "posek ha-dor," succeeded in combining in his personality exceptional scholarly genius, pioneering decisory ability in technological and medical fields, and noble qualities of humility and kindness that made him a rare consensus across all parts of Orthodox Judaism.[1, 2, 3, 4] His figure represents not only the continuity of the Heavenly Jerusalem, but also the ability of halakha to renew itself and respond to changing reality without losing its deep roots.

Chapter 1: Jerusalem Roots and the Growth of a Torah Giant

The growth of Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach is inseparably interwoven with the history of the Sha'arei Hesed neighborhood and Jerusalem within the walls. He was born on the 23rd of Tammuz 5670 (1910) as the first child in the Sha'arei Hesed neighborhood, which was founded by his maternal grandfather, Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Porush, after whom he was named.[3, 5, 6] His father, Rabbi Hayyim Yehuda Leib Auerbach, was a famous kabbalist and headed the kabbalists' yeshiva "Sha'ar ha-Shamayim." His mother, Rebbetzin Tzivya, was a daughter of the veteran Porush family.[5] The home in which he grew up was characterized by extreme material poverty but immense spiritual wealth; it is recounted that his parents sold their furniture to finance the yeshiva's debts, and the only moment when their spirits broke was when they were forced to sell books from their Torah library.[5]

Already in his youth, the extraordinary diligence of the young Shlomo Zalman was evident. A legendary story describes how on the day the first automobile entered Jerusalem, when all the yeshiva students went out to Jaffa Street to witness the marvel of the "carriage without horses," he remained the only one in the beit midrash, absorbed in his Talmud.[6] At age 11 he was already expert in the entire tractate Kiddushin, and continued his studies in the "Etz Hayyim" yeshiva under Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer, who became one of his primary teachers and praised his genius already in his youth.[2, 3, 6]

Recognition of his genius crossed sectors and boundaries. Despite his belonging to the Haredi public, Rabbi Auerbach felt tremendous respect for Maran Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak ha-Kohen Kook, who even arranged his wedding and served as sandek for his sons.[2, 3, 7] This relationship expressed Rabbi Auerbach's broad conception, which saw in Torah the supreme common denominator beyond political or ideological disputes.[9]

Chapter 2: The Technological Revolution and Halakha – "Me'orei Esh" as a Test Case

Rabbi Auerbach's most foundational contribution to the modern halakhic world began with the publication of his book "Me'orei Esh" (Luminaries of Fire) in 1935.[8] This book was the first comprehensive work that analyzed the nature of electricity through the lens of halakha, and received enthusiastic approbations from the generation's leading scholars, among them Rabbi Hayyim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna, who defined the author as one for whom "a new light shall shine upon Zion."[5, 6]

Rabbi Auerbach's method in investigating electricity was characterized by scientific thoroughness. He did not settle for theoretical knowledge, but sought to understand in depth the physical mechanisms of electric current, metal heating, and spark formation.[4] In contrast to the approach of the Hazon Ish, who saw closing an electrical circuit as constituting the prohibition of "boneh" (building), Rabbi Auerbach held that building the circuit itself does not constitute an act of acquisition or permanent construction, unless the action produces heat generation in an incandescent wire (the melakha of "mav'ir" [kindling]) or other melakhot.[10]

Another deep insight of Rabbi Auerbach concerned the use of electronic devices for sound transmission. He analyzed the operation of microphones and speakers and determined that one who hears the sound of a shofar or Megillah reading through them does not fulfill the obligation.[11] The halakhic-physical reasoning was original: once the sound is converted to electric current and reproduced by a membrane, it is no longer considered the person's original voice but rather a "sound of membrane vibrations."[11] This definition, written in the era of analog systems, remained a cornerstone even in the digital era, since the basic mechanism of converting sound to data and reconstructing it remains identical in its halakhic essence.[11]

His deep understanding of technology enabled him to rule on questions concerning the use of gerama (indirect causation) on Shabbat. He ruled that where there is need, such as opening doors with a magnetic card or using a hearing aid, one may rely on lenient approaches to using electricity that does not involve creating light or heat.[12] His halakhic realism was also expressed in his approach to the dynamic changes in the modern world, while maintaining meticulous decisory principles.

Chapter 3: Medical Ethics and Halakha – Pioneering Work and Complexity

Rabbi Auerbach is considered the father of halakhic medical ethics in the twentieth century. He worked in close cooperation with the Schlesinger Institute and was the central posek who shaped halakhic policy on issues of fertility, emergency medicine, and determination of the moment of death.[5, 6, 13] The books of his student, Rabbi Professor Avraham Sofer Avraham ("Nishmat Avraham"), and of Rabbi Yehoshua Neuwirth ("Shemirat Shabbat ke-Hilkhatah"), became the primary sources of information for observant physicians, with nearly every ruling in them having passed through HaGRaSh"Z's meticulous approval.[5, 6, 8]

Rulings on Fertility Issues and the Beginning of Life

Rabbi Auerbach displayed deep understanding of the distress of childless couples. He was among the first poskim to discuss extensively artificial insemination and advanced fertilization methods. In his halakhic approach, he permitted artificial insemination with the husband's sperm (AIH) in cases where there was no other way to conceive, and determined that the child is considered the husband's son for all purposes.[4] He even permitted taking birth control pills for a bride before her wedding to prevent huppat niddah (marriage during menstrual impurity), and permitted fertility tests involving various methods of obtaining sperm for the purpose of the mitzvah of procreation.[4]

Nevertheless, he established clear boundaries: he strongly opposed surrogacy and sperm donation from a Jew who is not the husband, out of concern for confusion in lineage and family structure.[4] His approach combined striving to solve the medical problem with preserving the sanctity of the Jewish family and the tradition of the generations.

Determining the Moment of Death and Organ Transplants

One of the most critical and complex junctures that Rabbi Auerbach addressed was the definition of death. He participated in committees and discussions of the Schlesinger Institute on the subject of brain death.[14] Although the subject remains intensely disputed among poskim, Rabbi Auerbach developed a methodology of examining signs of life and death according to clear physiological criteria, while understanding that this determination has life-and-death implications for those requiring organ transplants.[4, 13]

On the subject of treating terminally ill patients and premature infants, Rabbi Auerbach issued a famous and complex ruling: he permitted desecrating Shabbat for a premature infant whose chances of survival are slim, in order to preserve the value of life among the medical staff and public, and to prevent contempt for human life.[15] He distinguished between the "transient life" of a fetus or stillborn and a viable infant, and determined that
10 In situations where the suffering is infinite and there is no prospect for life, there is no halakhic obligation to prolong life through artificial means that intensify pain, but one must preserve the dignity and life of a person as long as there is breath in his nostrils.[15]

The level of detail into which Rabbi Auerbach descended was astonishing. His rulings dealt with the use of special spring beds for patients, the use of fans and comfort equipment for those hospitalized on Shabbat, and even the use of modern communications media (such as satellite and internet under certain conditions) for urgent medical needs.[4] He championed the principle that "Simplicity is Best" in solving complex problems, provided that the halakhic model remained rigorous.[4]

Chapter 4: The Commandments Dependent on the Land – The Shemitah Polemic and "Ma'adanei Eretz"

One of the areas in which Rabbi Auerbach's intellectual independence and halakhic courage stood out was the commandments dependent on the land. In 5649 he joined the kollel "Kerem Tzion" headed by Rabbi Tzvi Pesach Frank, where he deepened his study of complex agricultural matters.[5, 6] His books "Ma'adanei Eretz" on tractate Shevi'it (5704) and Terumot and Ma'asrot (5712) became the foundational modern works on the subject.[8, 16]

Rabbi Auerbach was known as one of the significant supporters of the "heter mekhirah" in the Haredi-Ashkenazi public.[6, 16] In his introduction to his book, he described how this dispensation was accepted by the great sages of Israel in previous generations and that it has solid foundations in the "mountains of holiness."[16, 17] He explained that although there is a great commandment to rest from working the land, in the reality of economic pikuah nefesh for the settlement, one may rely on the sale to a non-Jew which removes the sanctity of the land.[17]

His sensitivity to the public was evident in his ruling that one who purchases produce from a grocer who relies on the heter mekhirah does not transgress a prohibition, since in shemitah today (which is rabbinical according to most authorities) we follow the lenient position.[16, 17] He even instructed rabbis on behalf of the Chief Rabbinate how to execute the sale in the most meticulous manner legally and halakhically.[16] Nevertheless, he had tremendous appreciation for those who chose to be stringent upon themselves and to rest completely, provided that they would not impose their view on the broader public or disparage those who rely on the dispensation.[17]

The shemitah polemic placed Rabbi Auerbach at the center of the debate between the Haredi public (which mostly opposed the dispensation) and the Religious Zionist public. Rabbi Auerbach acted as a bridge, establishing the dispensation on classical scholarly tools and explaining that the great sages of the generations (such as Rabbi Kook and Rabbi Yitzhak Elhanan Spektor) did not act out of frivolity but out of heavy responsibility for the collective of Israel.[16, 18]

Chapter 5: The Rosh Yeshiva as Educator – "Students Are More Important than Books"

For 46 years, from 5709 until his death in 5755, Rabbi Auerbach served as rosh yeshiva of "Kol Torah" in Jerusalem.[3, 4, 19] This role was for him the core of his work, to such an extent that he refused to accept official rabbinical positions (such as the rabbinate of Jerusalem or a judgeship on the Great Rabbinical Court) in order to devote his time to his students.[3, 4]

His pedagogical approach was revolutionary in its simplicity and warmth. In contrast to the model of the distant rosh yeshiva, Rabbi Auerbach was accessible to every student, always showed a bright face, and spoke gently and with a smile.[19, 20] He believed that education must be based on love ("the right hand draws near") and that one should use "the left hand pushes away" (anger or punishment) only on extremely rare occasions.[19] He firmly opposed expelling weak students unless they posed a spiritual danger to others, and argued that the concept "one does not admit a student who is not proper" refers to adults and not to children or youths who need guidance.[19]

His method of teaching in his general lectures ("shiur kelali") was a model of clarity. He consciously avoided complex pilpul and intricate systems based on external brilliance, and preferred to delve deeply into the sugya while maintaining simplicity so that the students would emerge with a "clear Mishnah."[19] In examinations he conducted for students, he did not seek to make them fail or to test technical knowledge (such as "where is a particular word mentioned"), but rather sought to encourage them to review their Talmud and understand the sugya in depth.[19]

He used to say that "students are more important than books," when he explained why publication of his writings was delayed for many decades due to his devotion to education.[19] His influence reached its peak when hundreds of thousands of people, including thousands of his students, accompanied him on his final journey, in recognition that they had lost not only a posek but a spiritual father.[3, 7]

Chapter 6: Between Sectors and Groups – The Quiet Bridge of Jerusalem

Rabbi Auerbach was a unique figure in the Israeli landscape thanks to his ability to be accepted by all factions of religious and Haredi Judaism. Despite being deeply rooted in the Lithuanian Haredi world, he had tremendous respect for Maran Rabbi Kook and viewed him as a revered figure.[2, 3, 7] He would close his Gemara and run to peek into Rabbi Kook's room in order to see him learning, and testified that this viewing gave him strength for many weeks.[7]

His relationship to Religious Zionism and the State of Israel was complex and full of respect. Although he was not an ideological Zionist in the classical sense, he greatly appreciated the building of the land and the soldiers of the IDF.[9] He maintained continuous contact with the Chief Rabbis (Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu, Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, and others) and supported young men who chose to study in hesder yeshivot if it suited their character.[7] In his books he referred to Rabbi Kook with the title "mara de-ar'a kadisha" (master of the holy land), a rare expression in the Haredi public.[7]

He recoiled from politics and public controversies. In 5748, during the great schism in the Haredi public, he refused to express a position that might have increased polarization.[3] He emphasized the importance of "menschlichkeit" (humanity) as preceding any halakhic stringency. For example, he rebuked one of his family members who did not say "hello" to his niece for reasons of excessive modesty, and told him: "One must also be a human being."[21] His sensitivity to every Jew, secular as religious, was legendary; he would warmly bless taxi drivers and inquire after their families' welfare, and would enter to console mourners in the women's section in order to give them a sense of elevation and comfort.[20, 21]

Chapter 7: The Written Legacy and Its Influence on Subsequent Generations

Despite the fact that Rabbi Auerbach viewed the raising up of students as the essence of his work, the Torah literature he left behind is the backbone of the modern halakhic world. His books are characterized by a rare fusion of classical yeshiva scholarship with practical halakhic application.

Survey of His Major Works

Me'orei Esh (5695): The pioneering work on electricity on Shabbat. It opened the era in which halakhah confronts science with internal tools.[6, 8]

Ma'adanei Eretz (5704, 5712): A series of books on shemitah and terumot and ma'asrot, which constitutes the foundation for the study of commandments dependent on the land in our time.[8, 16]

Minhat Shlomo (volumes 1-3): A collection of responsa and articles on diverse topics, presenting the depth of his thought and his scientific-halakhic method.[5, 6, 8]

Halakhot Shlomo: A summary of his rulings and practices regarding the order of prayer, Shabbat, and the festivals. The book was edited by his grandsons and became a basic conduct manual in many homes.[8]

Shulhan Shlomo: A comprehensive compilation of his rulings according to the order of the Shulhan Arukh, enabling rapid access to his decisions in all areas of life.[8]

In addition, his influence is evident through books written under his auspices. "Shemirat Shabbat Ke-Hilkhatah" by Rabbi Neuwirth is probably the most influential book on Jewish Shabbat observance in the last hundred years.[5, 6, 8] Part 3 of the second edition includes corrections and additions in Rabbi Auerbach's handwriting, which constitute a critical layer in modern Shabbat halakhic decision-making.[8]

Chapter 8: Summary and Analysis of His Character as "Posek of the Generation"

Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach was not merely a rabbi or rosh yeshiva; he was a symbol of the ability of Orthodox Judaism to flourish within a changing world without compromising a single iota. The secret of his appeal lay in the paradoxical combination of genius and simplicity, rigor and gentleness, conservatism and innovation.

His teaching
His halakhic teaching demonstrated that reality is not an enemy of halakhah, but rather an arena in which it is called upon to manifest itself. His method of analyzing technological issues (such as electricity) or medical ones (such as fertility) proved that the study of Torah with integrity and clarity can provide an answer to every human question. His educational leadership at the yeshivah "Kol Torah" presented an alternative of love and patience in an era that was sometimes characterized by excessive rigidity.

Above all, Rabbi Auerbach represented the concept of "torat ḥesed" (Torah of loving-kindness). His work on behalf of the sick, the elderly, women, and children demonstrated that greatness in Torah and greatness in character traits are one and the same.[22] For generations of rabbis, physicians, and students, the figure of HaGRaSHaZ will always remain the lighthouse illuminating the path of walking in the ways of the Torah while seeing the face of the human being.[3, 4, 9] His legacy is not only in his books, but in the thousands of "living books"—his students and those who continue his path—who continue to illuminate the Jewish world with his unique light.
